articles.title: A mother who had to quit her Rs 50 LPA job, now changing chess scene in North India
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Have you ever visited a chess tournament? There is a certain kind of silence that persists outside a tournament hall. It belongs to the parents.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Have you ever visited a chess tournament? There is a certain kind of silence that persists outside a tournament hall. It belongs to the parents. Behind the doors, children are hunched over boards in a hush so complete you can hear clocks being slapped. Outside, in the corridor, adults sit with water bottles and phones they are not really looking at, waiting for a result that will arrive as a small face in a doorway, either lit or collapsed.Most people spend those hours waiting. Nidhi Bhasin Rohilla was once one among them before she finally huffed, "This is not my cup of tea."Today, the enterprise she has built from the hours of pondering in those noiseless corridors runs events across eight states, more than 40 a month, with about 16 paid staff and roughly 100 volunteers.Nevertheless, it all began with a corporate salesperson who had to choose between her career and her daughter's.The choiceShivika Rohilla, Nidhi's elder daughter, started playing chess in September 2013, aged six and a half. By April next year, she was second at the Delhi State Championship in her age group."We realised that she had achieved this in less than six months of playing chess. That was when we decided to focus more seriously on chess," Nidhi told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction.Nidhi, a dentist by degree, had built a sales career at different top-tier corporate institutions. Her husband, a surgeon, worked at AIIMS Delhi.In 2012-13, Delhi, by her count, had "perhaps only three or four good" chess coaches."We wanted to ensure that Shivika received the right coaching, even if that meant taking her outside Delhi," Shivika's mother shared.With both parents busy earning the fund needed to fuel Shivika’s budding chess career, there was little time for them to travel with her to tournaments."As she started performing well, people recommended that if we wanted her to achieve the required norms and titles, we would need to take her abroad since India did not have enough tournaments of the level required for players pursuing Grandmaster titles," she added. "Initially, I sent my mother with Shivika to participate in these tournaments."The turning point came when Shivika was about 12 and hit a bad stretch. "She was unhappy with her performance and started losing games," Nidhi continued. "Part of the problem was that travelling to South India for coaching regularly was not financially or practically feasible for us. We were managing with the coaching available in Delhi."The coaching was there, but the environment was not. Her school, St. Mary's, had little chess culture, and her friends had mostly quit.Nidhi recalled, "Eventually, she started questioning whether she should continue playing chess. She would ask, 'Why should I continue? What opportunities are there in chess?"At that time, I had to choose between my career and Shivika's chess career. Obviously, when a child has to travel for tournaments, one parent needs to accompany them. That was when I decided I needed to step back from my own career and give her the support she required."The ponderingJust before the COVID pandemic, Nidhi, who was earning around Rs 50 lakh per annum at that time, left her job for good. "I realised that Shivika needed to travel more frequently. Her rating had reached nearly 2,000, and the next step was to work towards achieving the norms and titles she was pursuing," she recalled."We were spending a tremendous amount of money. We had no external financial support, and everything had to be managed by my husband and me. Our savings were being depleted. Almost everything we earned was going towards chess."The family was getting closer and closer to calling it an end. But a final shot was awaiting as they took Shivika to a top tournament in Brazil, treating it as a verdict."If she performed well and we felt she had a real chance of progressing, we would continue supporting her. Otherwise, we would reconsider our decision," she revealed.Shivika was among the top five in her category. "Her games went well, and people were appreciating her performance," Nidhi said. It was not a full stop after all.Eventually, Shivika's father left salaried work and opened his own hospital."A regular salary is often insufficient to support a serious chess career unless the family has substantial financial resources," Nidhi said. "Some coaches charge Rs 4,000-5,000 per hour."The gapThen came the problem that created the growing chess ecosystem. During Shivika's year off after Class 12, the family paid practice partners Rs 2,000-3,000 an hour."To prepare for games against International Masters and Grandmasters, she needed strong practice opponents who could push her to improve," Nidhi recalled.But, Shivika would mostly beat these practice partners, raising eyebrows of those around her. Therefore, her family felt she was not gaining as much from the sessions as they had hoped.Delhi didn't have enough top-quality players in one place. So Nidhi built one."We wanted to create opportunities for players to meet in cafés and play meaningful practice games," she revealed. There came the Chess Coffee Connect initiative by SR Chess Academy.The idea behind the academy, SRCA, grew from the coaches already working with Shivika. "Since I was already paying for Shivika's coaching, we could use the same arrangement to help other children learn," Nidhi explained.It started with two or three children. Today it has nearly 80."We did not have a website or a formal setup at the beginning. We had a space, a coach, chess books, and Shivika's equipment," Nidhi recalled with a smile.Chess Coffee Connect, the café-based circuit, followed as the answer to the same loneliness that nearly pushed Shivika out of the game.South India, Nidhi feels, has the advantage of community, where players travel together and "analyse their mistakes immediately after playing."Delhi did not have it. "We need to develop a culture in which people continue playing chess and support one another," she added.Now, hundreds of players/chess enthusiasts meet at a particular place almost every week to play games, share ideas, and build a community the north was lacking.Listening as strategyHer explanation of the growth that her ventures have seen has little to do with marketing, despite a career spent in it."I work from the heart and maintain a strong connection with the players," she revealed. "Our principle is simple. We listen to what people need and try to provide it."The results read like a list of complaints turned into products. Parents wanted a 25+5 time control for practice before rated events, so she created one. Senior citizens couldn't afford weekly entries, so there is a discount. Mothers said their daughters weren't getting support from their fathers to play, so those girls play free.Through the Helping Hands NGO, some children get free books and classes. Nidhi, however, feels that keeping them in the game is hard: "It can be difficult for them to justify continuing to invest their limited resources."The portfolio has since spread. There are chess-learning cards, including a Grandmaster series she says is trademarked.There is a sports-psychology arm, Mind to Moves, which runs sessions for parents on rating anxiety before major tournaments.There is a Chess Moms Club, born from watching parents guard information about coaches and events.What Delhi was missingSome of the most telling work isn't aimed at prodigies."We now have senior citizens who come to Chess Coffee Connect and tell us that they played chess in school but have not had an opportunity to play regularly for years," she said, overjoyed. "When they return to the game, it makes everything worthwhile."Besides various theme-based events, the organisation has also hosted a game between a visually impaired player and a sighted one."Chess is a game. It is not only about tournaments, ratings, or winning titles. If a child plays because they genuinely love chess, they may continue enjoying it throughout their lives," she noted.The unfinished partFor all the scale, the finances remain stubbornly homemade."Sponsorship is our biggest challenge," she revealed. "We currently have no sponsors, and everything is self-funded."Chess.com's yearly free memberships were the only notable outside help. Federations have been supportive, she feels. But the bigger issue is cost, as she added, "Venues do not provide their facilities for free.""My knowledge of sales, marketing, negotiation, and working with organisations has helped me approach schools and other institutions." But she says she hasn't had to push hard, as invitations came through the front door.Meanwhile, Shivika, now a Woman International Master (WIM), is studying aerospace engineering in London, a five-year course she settled on in Class 7 or 8, and she hasn't stopped playing. She recently won a tournament there.The family has taken the model with her. Chess Coffee Connect has run eight ECF-rated events in England.Asked whether she is satisfied with the work she has managed to do for chess, Nidhi doesn't pretend to be finished. "I could not be happier with what we have accomplished. However, I know there is always more we can do."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Lightning star Nikita Kucherov reportedly requests trade from Tampa Bay; GM says they have 'no intention' of trading him
articles.summary: Kucherov reportedly told his Tampa Bay teammates about his request while on the team plane on Friday.
articles.body:
Tampa Bay Lightning right wing Nikita Kucherov has reportedly requested a trade, becoming the latest high-profile NHL player to ask to leave his longtime home.

Kucherov, 33, has informed the Lightning that he will not be re-signing with the team, per multiple reports.

Kucherov also told his teammates about the move, reportedly sharing the news while on the team plane, per The Athletic's Pierre LeBrun . Tampa Bay plays the Nashville Predators in Tennessee on Saturday.

In a statement on Friday, general manager Julien Brisebois said that the team is "aware" of reports that Kucherov wants out but said that they don't have plans to trade him.

"We unequivocally have no intention of trading Nikita," Brisebois wrote.

Kucherov, the reigning Hart Trophy winner (the NHL's league MVP trophy), is currently in the final year of an eight-year, $76 million contract and is set to become an unrestricted free agent this offseason. However, talks on a potential extension have not progressed much, per multiple reports, leading to Kucherov's request.

Per LeBrun , Kucherov will continued playing with Tampa Bay while awaiting a trade.

The Russian winger has spent his entire NHL career with the Lightning, after being selected by the team 58th overall in the 2011 draft. He became an alternate captain for the team in 2022.

Kucherov has won the Hart Trophy twice in his career (2019, 2026) and helped lead Tampa Bay to two Stanley Cup championships in 2020 and 2021. He's led the league in scoring three times, taking home the Art Ross Trophy in 2019, 2024 and 2025.

Despite his recent success, Kucherov is looking to find a new home after 15 years. Per LeBrun , Kucherov does not have a full no-trade clause in his contract, and has provided a 10-team list of approved destinations to the Lightning.

Kucherov is just the latest player to express his desire to be traded: Last week, the Winnipeg Jets traded Connor Hellebuyck to the New Jersey Devils, ending a saga where Hellebuyck got suspended and lost $930,000 of his salary. Meanwhile, the Detroit Red Wings are in the middle of a similar saga with forward Dylan Larkin, with the team suspending Larkin on Thursday amid his demands for a trade.

articles.title: JuJu Watkins says she's dreamed of her first basket since ACL injury as USC looks to end title drought
articles.summary: JuJu Watkins returns to USC women's basketball after rehabbing an ACL tear, joining Jazzy Davidson in a loaded backcourt chasing a national title.
articles.body: JuJu Watkins, one of the brightest young stars in women’s college basketball, is back on the court. The Southern California guard was sidelined last season while rehabbing a torn ACL. Watkins' first two seasons with the USC Trojans saw her score an average of 25.6 points per game. Now, she returns to a talented supporting cast as the No. 3 Trojans pursue their first national championship since 1984. "It’s on my mind every day," Watkins said. "So much anticipation has gone into this year. I want it really badly, but also in a healthy way. I just want to have fun and really enjoy this year." PACERS STAR TYRESE HALIBURTON MOVED TO TEARS AFTER LONG-AWAITED RETURN FROM ACHILLES INJURY Watkins added that she's already imagined what it will feel like to see her first basket go in. "I’ve had dreams about that every night. I might shed a tear, honestly, I can’t lie," she said. "That’ll be a really amazing feeling for me." Watkins scored 18 points in 22 minutes during USC’s recent exhibition win over California, offering an early glimpse of what her return could mean. She will share the backcourt with Big Ten Freshman of the Year Jazzy Davidson, who averaged 17.9 points last season. Although this will be their first season playing together, the duo began building chemistry while Watkins recovered from the injury she suffered in the second round of the 2025 NCAA Tournament. She could often be seen encouraging Davidson from the sideline. NEW FACES, NEW PLACES: FIVE TRANSFER PORTAL PLAYERS POISED FOR SUCCESS THIS COMING SEASON "She saw me being hard on myself and I think she saw a little bit of her in me," Davidson said, "and so she kind of knew what it was like going through that. Being able to build the friendship that we were able to build, it’s a huge blessing." USC’s stockpile of talent includes guard Saniyah Hall, who had 23 points, six rebounds and five steals in the Trojans’ exhibition, as well as forward Sara Okeke, one of three five-star recruits to join the roster. "They have proven that they’re going to be really impactful players at a high level," coach Lindsay Gottlieb said. Last season, Watkins would set up chairs in the locker room for the team talk on the road. It was one of the small ways she found to be useful without being on the court. "I was able to take on a leadership role for sure, and I can’t say I really owned that role prior to that," she said. "Being able to do that and also see the game from a different perspective and seeing how can I help my team really helped grow my IQ and leadership skills." articles.title: “She always put others first and encouraged me”: How Naomi Osaka’s mom backed her tennis dreams by working long hours while her father taught both sisters the game
articles.summary: Naomi Osaka’s rise to the top of tennis came with years of work behind it.
articles.body: Naomi Osaka’s rise to the top of tennis came with years of work behind it. Her parents, Tamaki Osaka and Leonard François, played very different roles in that journey. While her mother worked hard to support the family and pay for her daughters’ tennis ambitions, her father took charge of their early training despite having little experience with the sport.Their efforts helped Naomi and her older sister, Mari, get the chance to pursue tennis from a young age. And Naomi has never hidden how much she owes them. Naomi Osaka’s mother Tamaki worked long hours to support her daughters’ tennis dreamsNaomi has often spoken about her mother’s sacrifices. In a statement shared with People in May 2021, the four-time Grand Slam champion recalled watching Tamaki work hard to support her passion for tennis.“Growing up, I saw my mother work incredibly hard to support me and my passion for play,” Naomi said. She also added, “She always put others first and encouraged me to embrace my diversity.”Tamaki’s work went beyond simply cheering from the sidelines. She helped support the family financially while Naomi and Mari trained and competed. The costs of developing two young tennis players included equipment, court access and travel. Tamaki took on long working hours to help meet those demands. Naomi later spoke about seeing her mother push through exhaustion, an image that stayed with her as she grew older.There was also a personal side to Tamaki’s support. Naomi grew up in a Japanese-Haitian household, with her mother helping her stay connected to her Japanese roots. The family eventually chose to have Naomi represent Japan, even though she grew up in the United States.For Naomi, her mother’s influence was not limited to tennis. Tamaki encouraged her to accept her background and feel comfortable with her identity. That support became part of the foundation behind the player fans know today. Leonard François followed Richard Williams’ example to coach Naomi and Mari OsakaWhile Tamaki helped make the tennis journey possible, Leonard François took responsibility for teaching his daughters the game. His decision came after watching Venus and Serena Williams compete at the 1999 French Open.Leonard saw similarities between the Williams sisters and his own daughters. He also studied how their father, Richard Williams, had guided their careers. Although Leonard had little tennis experience, he began learning the sport through instructional books and videos before coaching Naomi and Mari.“The blueprint was already there. I just had to follow it,” Leonard told in 2018.The family moved from Japan to Long Island in 2000, when Naomi was three. Leonard then put both girls through demanding practice sessions, with thousands of balls hit as they worked on their game. He later helped move the family to Florida to give them better training opportunities.His role did not end when Naomi became a professional. In October 2019, after her father coached her during tournaments in Osaka and Beijing, Naomi spoke about their relationship in a post-match press conference. She joked that he annoyed her enough to make her angry, which she then used as motivation to win.But she also made her affection clear in a post on X on October 10, 2019. Naomi wrote that she loved her father and felt grateful for everything she learned from him, both on and off the court.Tamaki’s hard work helped provide the opportunity. Leonard’s decision to teach himself tennis gave Naomi and Mari their first lessons. Their approaches were different, but both parents helped build the path that Naomi would eventually take to the top of the sport.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Illinois high school advances in football playoff after record-breaking 88-84 win, temporary suspension due to darkness
articles.summary: The high-scoring matchup in Chicago ended with 172 total points, with the winning quarterback throwing for more than 650 yards and 8 touchdowns (a state reco...
articles.body:
A high school football game in Chicago turned into a wildly high-scoring affair. On Friday, Quincy Senior High School defeated Sarah E. Goode STEM Academy 88-84 in the first round of Illinois' 6A high school football playoffs.

Besides having 172 total points — breaking an Illinois state record — the matchup also had a stoppage to switch fields after it was suspended due to darkness.

Per the Illinois High School Association (IHSA), the game was originally supposed to take place on Saturday, but was switched to Friday afternoon at 3 p.m. CT. The Blue Devils had to drive more than 300 miles from Quincy, which is located southwest of Chicago on the Missouri border, to Chicago for the matchup, and requested the Friday time to save on hotel costs.

Quincy entered the matchup as a No. 9 seed, with No. 8-seeded Sarah E. Goode hosting the game at their stadium in southern Chicago. Goode held a narrow 60-59 lead at halftime after a two-hour offensive slugfest in the first half; officials shortened the halftime to just six minutes to try and save daylight since the field did not have lights, per Muddy River Sports' Matt Schuckman .

Unfortunately, the game had to be suspended with 3:42 remaining due to darkness, with the call coming just before 6 p.m. local time. The two teams then to relocated to the field of nearby Englewood STEM High School, which has lights.

Per the IHSA, it took an hour to transport the two teams there and let them warm up before the game resumed. Quincy, holding a 88-84 lead, recovered an onside kick after the restart, and opted to run out the final minutes of the game for the win. In all, the game lasted more than four hours, including time it took to switch fields.

Junior Quincy quarterback Bryson Little threw for more than 650 yards in the contest, throwing a state-record eight touchdown passes and adding two more scores on the ground. Meanwhile, for Goode, senior running back Aedan Cleveland picked up more than 300 rushing yards with five rushing touchdowns.

The 172 total points scored breaks an Illinois state record of 166 points, set in 2021. With the win, Quincy advances to the second round of the playoffs, which will resume next weekend.

articles.title: Red Wings Trade Pitch Replaces Dylan Larkin With $14 Million Minnesota Center
articles.summary: A Detroit Red Wings trade proposal sends captain Dylan Larkin to the Minnesota Wild in exchange for a package featuring a $14 million center. The post Red Wi...
articles.body:
The Dylan Larkin drama reached a crescendo on Thursday when the 12-year veteran informed the Detroit Red Wings that he would no longer show up to play for them as long as his trade request went unmet, and the team responded by suspending Larkin without pay.

But a new trade pitch published Friday would solve the Larkin problem, and replace him with an eight-year veteran center from the Minnesota Wild in a deal that would also send Detroit a pair of first-round draft picks and a 22-year-old winger who was, himself, a Wild first-round pick.

Larkin would land with Minnesota under the trade pitch that would cost the Wild Danila Yurov, Yakov Trenin and two first-round picks.

With Larkin suspended without pay for refusing to play, Detroit must decide whether a package built on youth and draft capital is enough for its top center.

The idea comes from a trade proposal posted to PuckGM . The swap adds a net $4.228 million to Minnesota's cap and removes the same amount from Detroit's.

Larkin, 30, was born July 30, 1996, in Waterford, Michigan. Detroit drafted him 15th overall in 2014 after a freshman season at the University of Michigan. He owns 278 goals and 649 points in 818 games, including five consecutive 30-goal seasons. His eight-year, $69.6 million deal ending 2030-31 pays $8.7 million annually and includes a full no-trade clause through 2027-28. He is forfeiting roughly $41,237 per day in salary during the suspension.

Yurov, 22, was born Dec. 22, 2003, in Chelyabinsk, Russia, and Minnesota drafted him 24th overall in 2022. He won a Gagarin Cup with Metallurg Magnitogorsk in 2024 before signing an entry-level contract in May 2025. He recorded 12 goals and 27 points in 73 games as a rookie and has four goals in 15 games this season . His entry-level deal runs through the 2027-28 season , after which he becomes a restricted free agent.

Trenin, 29, was born Jan. 13, 1997, in Chelyabinsk, and Nashville drafted him 55th overall in 2015. He has 61 goals and 122 points in 472 games with Nashville, Colorado and Minnesota , mostly as a physical penalty killer. His four-year, $14 million contract signed in 2024 pays $3.5 million annually through 2027-28. Minnesota has shopped him for cap flexibility , according to Pro Hockey Rumors .

Minnesota has long coveted Larkin as a missing piece , according to The Athletic , and the Wild have sent multiple offers to Detroit , The Hockey News reported. One earlier concept featured a package of three first-round picks , according to NHL Insight . Detroit has not accepted any of them.

Larkin's list of approved trade destinations answers the question of whether the three-time All-Star would accept the deal. Minnesota remains on Larkin's expanded 10-team list , joining Vegas, Florida and seven other clubs. The Wild, Panthers and Golden Knights made Larkin's original three-team preferred list , according to the Star Tribune .

Financially, the deal raises Minnesota's payroll by $4.228 million against a $104 million ceiling, even after Trenin's $3.5 million leaves. Competitively, Larkin gives the Wild a No. 1 center beside Kirill Kaprizov, Matt Boldy, Joel Eriksson Ek and Quinn Hughes.

Red Wings Dylan Larkin Trade Return and Rebuild

Detroit receives a cost-controlled center in Yurov, a physical depth forward in Trenin and two first-round selections. The Red Wings also end the distracting Larkin standoff.

Minnesota gets the larger immediate gain in a top-line center signed through 2030-31 for picks and one prospect.

Detroit gets cap flexibility, youth and draft capital, a return that supports a retool more than a full teardown. The trade resolves the Larkin conundrum for both clubs, while the Red Wings still have to weigh whether it is the best return available from a limited list of suitors.

articles.title: Nebraska soccer falls in season finale to Purdue 2-1
articles.summary: Nebraska concluded the 2026 season on Friday at Purdue. The Huskers fell short once again, ending the season with a 2-1 defeat.
articles.body:
Nebraska soccer (3-5-10, 1-4-7 Big Ten) concluded the 2026 season on Friday night at Purdue (15-2-2, 9-2-1 Big Ten). The Huskers fell short once again, ending the season with a 2-1 defeat to the Boilermakers.

Nebraska initially took the lead in the second half, scoring on a penalty kick in the 54th minute. Purdue responded, however, delivering the equalizer on a penalty kick in the 63rd minute before hitting the go-ahead score in the 86th minute. Ella Guyott scored for the Huskers on the penalty kick, her only shot on the night.

The Boilermakers outshot the Huskers 18-13 on the night. Purdue especially brought the pressure in the second half, with the team firing 12 in the 45-minute stretch. The Boilermakers also topped Nebraska in shots on goal, 5-4.

Carson Bohonek led the Huskers in shooting, totaling four in the loss, two on goal. Ava Makovicka finished with three shots, one on goal. Avery Gillahan earned three saves in the loss, going 3-for-5 in shots faced.

Nebraska, unfortunately, misses out on the Big Ten Tournament after going 3-5-10 on the regular season. The Huskers' 10 ties lead the nation, alongside Loyola-Maryland. Nebraska also earned nine shutouts on the season, only two shy of the nation's best this year.

articles.title: Piketon football advances to Week 12, Huntington falls to Covington
articles.summary: Piketon football handed Meigs a loss in Division V, Region 19 play while Huntington saw its season come to a close in Division VI, Region 24.
articles.body:
The Redstreaks are moving onto Week 12 after traveling to Pomeroy to earn a hard-fought victory over Meigs.

Piketon (7-4) found itself in a 7-0 hole after giving up an early touchdown.

But with 5:48 left in the second quarter, Nolan Childers found Tristen Bodicker for a 14-yard touchdown pass to tie the score.

Meigs took a 13-7 lead early in the third, but with just five minutes left in the game, Tanner Loar scored from a yard out to give the 'Streaks a one-point lead. Braxton Walters then put the win on ice with an interception.

Childers finished 5-for-6 passing for 105 yards and a score, Bodicker had two receptions for 25 yards and a touchdown, and Loar carried the ball 23 times for 106 yards and the game-winning trip to the end zone.

Piketon will now prepare to travel to Fort Frye in Week 12. That game is scheduled for a 7 p.m. kickoff, Nov. 6.

After taking a 20-13 lead into halftime, Huntington (7-4) surrendered 22 unanswered points in a Division VI, Region 24 first-round playoff contest.

The Huntsmen got on the board with a 32-yard touchdown pass from Frankie Hirsch to LJ Cooper to take a 7-0 lead with just under 10 minutes to play in the first quarter. They'd take a 13-0 lead — following a missed PAT — when Hirsch found the end zone from 50 yards out.

Covington answered with two straight scores, forcing a 13-13 tie, but Hirsch recovered a fumble just before halftime and found the end zone for a third time, giving his team a lead at the break.

In the third, the Buccaneers found a rhythm quickly, taking a 21-20 lead with a two-point try, scoring again with a lengthy drive and delivering the final score on an interception return for a touchdown.

Hirsch led Huntington's efforts statistically, finishing 8-of-19 passing for 119 yards and a score, alongside 12 rushes for 102 yards and a touchdown. He also recovered a fumble and returned it for a score.

Cooper ended the night with five catches for 106 yards and a score.

articles.title: Sam Houston leans on Jaidon Hamilton, rolls into bye week with win over Highlands
articles.summary: The running back rushed for 133 yards and a pair of touchdowns, and the Hurricanes defense bottled up Highlands to earn the win headed into an open week.
articles.body:
Coming off an emotional win over Harlandale, Sam Houston coach Rashard Colquitt knew the Hurricanes' matchup against Highlands had trap game written all over it.

Colquitt wanted his team to finish its regular season strong, though, and head into a much-needed open week riding a six-game win streak.

Beat up and with its pass game off rhythm, Sam Houston leaned on junior Jaidon Hamilton and a stout defensive performance as the Hurricanes rolled past the Owls 33-14 Friday at Alamo Stadium.

"We just had to finish," Colquitt said. "That was the main goal. We knew Highlands was going to give us their best shot. They had a week off. So they had two weeks to prepare for us. We haven't had a bye week. Our bye week is next week. So I knew it was going to be tough.

"But I'm proud of our guys. We're tired. We're beat up a little bit. So for our guys to come out and still perform at a high level, it just shows the preparation our coaches and players are putting in. We're happy to get this win."

After a long punt return from senior Treston Zacharie, paired with a face mask penalty, junior Xavier Youngblood only needed one play to put Sam Houston on the board. Youngblood took a direct snap out to his right for the 5-yard score.

On third-and-14, Hurricanes junior Jaelyn Turner picked off Highlands senior Johnathon Cantu near midfield to set up Sam Houston's second scoring drive.

The Hurricanes quickly moved into the Owls' red zone off a pair of rushes from Hamilton, and Youngblood's first completion of the night. A high snap allowed Highlands defenders to sink towards Youngblood, but he was still able to get the hand off to Hamilton. Senior Sincere Brown laid a key block that cleared the way for Hamilton to walk in untouched for a 13-yard score.

"Our offensive line did a great job of opening up some holes for Jaidon," Colquitt said. "He had some big runs."

The Owls entered the second quarter trailing by two possessions, and life didn't get much easier as Sam Houston junior Aidan Ward ripped through Highlands' offensive line and forced an errant throw from Cantu that was picked off by senior Reginald Mackall.

Two plays later, Hamilton broke free for a 55-yard rush down to the Owls' 1-yard line. Youngblood punched in his second rushing touchdown of the night on fourth down, but a missed extra point kept Sam Houston leading 20-0.

Cantu put Highlands on the board with a 24-yard rushing touchdown late in the second quarter, and the Owls went into halftime trailing by 13. Sam Houston came out of halftime intentionally trying to get Youngblood settled in. Colquitt dialed up quick, easy completions for his junior QB as the Hurricanes marched down the field. Hamilton capped off the drive with a 15-yard touchdown scamper.

He finished the game with 133 rushing yards and a pair of touchdowns on 12 carries.

"I knew my team needed me," Hamilton said. "So I came out here and just did what I do."

Highlands (1-8, 1-6) scored its second and final touchdown off a 61-yard rush from sophomore Darrius Long.

But Youngblood shook off his earlier struggles and finally got one over on an Owls defense set on denying him the long ball. The quarterback connected with junior Mario Ringo for a 52-yard touchdown to seal the game.

The Hurricanes (8-2, 7-1) could still claim a share of the District 14-5A-II title if Harlandale beats McCollum next week in the Frontier Bowl. But the chance to rest and reset before the playoffs is top of mind for Sam Houston next week.

"Now we can teach the fundamental things," Colquitt said. "I think that's going to help us and propel us in this playoff run we're trying to make."

articles.title: Ryan Blaney needs major run at Martinsville to keep title hopes alive
articles.summary: Ryan Blaney needs a major run in the NASCAR Cup Series race at Martinsville Speedway to keep his title hopes alive.
articles.body:
Ryan Blaney's NASCAR Cup Series championship hopes suffered a devastating blow during Sunday's YellaWood 500 at Talladega Superspeedway. The Team Penske driver started 27th and finished 38th after a major accident eliminated him during the second stage.

Blaney entered Talladega fifth in the championship standings, trailing Kyle Larson by 40 points with three races remaining. His afternoon initially appeared promising as he worked through the field and finished eighth in Stage 1, earning valuable championship points.

However, Blaney's race ended suddenly on Lap 132 when he lost momentum while running behind teammate Joey Logano in the outside drafting lane. The resulting contact and traffic disruption triggered a 12-car accident involving several championship contenders.

Blaney's No. 12 Ford sustained significant damage, preventing him from continuing after completing 131 laps. The early retirement left him 38th and limited his points total to four.

Blaney dropped one position to sixth in the NASCAR Cup Series Chase standings with 2,334 points. He now trails championship leader Kyle Larson by 107 points, a substantial increase from his pre-race deficit. Although Blaney remains mathematically eligible for the championship, he faces an extremely difficult task entering the final two races at Martinsville and Homestead-Miami.

articles.title: Knicks’ Jalen Brunson calls out Josh Hart for fatigue comments

articles.body:
Jalen Brunson always has a thing or two up his sleeve to take shots at his teammate Josh Hart . The star point guard recently had a lighthearted response to Hart's admission that the New York Knicks are already feeling the effects of fatigue early in the 2026-27 season.

After the Knicks lost 98-93 to the Philadelphia 76ers on Friday, Brunson was asked about Hart's comments. He joked that his teammate's age might explain why he is feeling tired just six games into the campaign.

"Josh said he feels the fatigue? Well, Josh is old as s–t, so," Brunson told reporters.

Hart had acknowledged the team's physical struggles following the loss. The Knicks have played a demanding schedule after reaching the end of last season in June, leaving them with a shorter offseason than other teams.

"We all feel the fatigue, but we have to fight through it. Six games in, we have to make sure we get our bodies ready to play every day," Hart earlier said. "I think mentally, we're there. We just got to find it physically."

Hart also entered the season dealing with a finger injury that he cannot have surgically repaired until he retires. Despite that issue, he has continued to play as New York tries to find consistency.

The loss in Philadelphia dropped the defending champions to 2-4. The Knicks had started the season 0-3 after raising their championship banner, before earning consecutive wins over the Detroit Pistons and Chicago Bulls. However, they have now lost twice to the 76ers this season.

articles.title: Imanol Alguacil Reveals Secret Behind Olympiacos' Strong Start
articles.summary: Imanol Alguacil revealed the secret behind Olympiacos' strong start to Magenta TV, saying "the secret lies in the excellent work of everyone" at the club.
articles.body:
Imanol Alguacil revealed to Magenta TV the secret of his good start at Olympiacos , also referring to the match against Kifisia.

In detail, what Alguacil told Magenta TV was about whether he expected such a good start on the Olympiacos bench: "Well, I didn't imagine it. Or at least I hadn't calculated it in numbers. But I knew Olympiacos always had to win. When a team is chasing titles in three competitions and even starts as the favorite in all three, it is obvious that it must win matches.

"The secret lies in the excellent work of everyone: the players, the coaching staff, and the people who work at Renti. Because a coach, without all these people, is nothing."

On the match against Kifisia, he said: "It will be a difficult and demanding match. We are facing a tough rival that always makes things difficult for Olympiacos, especially when we play at their stadium."

We know we must give our best. Fortunately, we can make many changes to the lineup, which allows us to approach every match, even if we play every three days, with rested players.

Our objective against Kifisia is to maintain the strong results we have achieved in Europe, the league, and the Cup. However, we know that to achieve this, we must give our best.

On whether he also has the match against Rennes in mind: "No, because sometimes we play with three days of rest and other times with two. It doesn't affect us at all. Fortunately, this particular match, even though it is away from home, is very close to the scheduled date. For the match against Rennes, they moved the kickoff time earlier, so we will return with enough time to rest. I always say that we must not look for excuses."

"We have to adapt, and that is precisely what we are doing as the calendar changes. We have to approach every match as if it were the last and give everything we have with the players we have available."

On whether he has problems with absences, he said: "Let's be realistic. The truth is that all the players are responding very well. I am very happy because this shows the good work the medical staff is doing, but also the players themselves, who take great care of themselves and work systematically to prevent injuries."

"At the moment, we are very fortunate that everyone is available, and that is the best news for a coach. I had to leave two players out of the squad, Scipioni and Clayton, who are performing very well. But I had to leave them out precisely because all the players are available."

articles.title: Ty Gibbs eliminated from Cup championship contention in 2026

The Joe Gibbs Racing driver qualified eighth and entered the race hoping to strengthen his position in the NASCAR Cup Series championship Chase.

Gibbs began the afternoon with favorable track position but was unable to secure stage points during the opening segment. His race became more complicated on Lap 132 when a 12-car accident erupted in the outside drafting lane.

Gibbs was among the competitors collected, sustaining damage that affected his ability to remain competitive. Unlike several other Chase contenders, he was able to continue racing, but the damage and lost track position prevented him from mounting a serious challenge for the victory.

Gibbs ultimately completed 188 laps, finishing 17th and one lap behind winner Kyle Larson. The result earned him 20 points and moved him to ninth in the NASCAR Cup Series Chase standings, tied with Austin Cindric at 2,258 points.

However, Gibbs trails Larson by 183 points with only two races remaining, mathematically eliminating him from championship contention. Gibbs will now focus on improving his final standing at Martinsville and Homestead-Miami while attempting to finish his season with stronger results.

articles.summary: William Byron has been eliminated from contention in the Chase for the 2026 NASCAR Cup Series championship.

William Byron narrowly missed his first victory of the 2026 NASCAR Cup Series season on Sunday, finishing second in the YellaWood 500 at Talladega Superspeedway. The Hendrick Motorsports driver started 17th and worked his way into contention before crossing the finish line just 0.041 seconds behind teammate Kyle Larson.

Byron was among the strongest competitors throughout the afternoon, finishing fifth in both stages while maintaining a presence near the front of the field. His Chevrolet avoided the significant damage that eliminated several championship contenders in two multicar accidents.

The final lap presented Byron with an opportunity to steal the victory. He made a move beneath Ricky Stenhouse Jr. entering the tri-oval, but Larson carried additional momentum along the bottom lane and surged ahead before the finish line.

Despite missing the victory, Byron earned his season-best finish and helped Hendrick Motorsports secure the top two positions. He also made significant progress in the NASCAR Cup Series Chase standings, climbing three positions to 11th with 2,227 points.

However, the 214-point deficit to championship leader Larson mathematically eliminates Byron from title contention with two races remaining. He will look to finish the season strongly at Martinsville Speedway and Homestead-Miami Speedway.
